svg.title: Wireframe: whole page overview (desktop 1280px)

g.text: Fewer Australians are dying on the roads. The number being
seriously hurt hasn't fallen. We went through a decade of
hospital records to find out who is being hurt, and how badly.
For every road death in 2021, 35 people were admitted to hospital
Notes: Source: BITRE hospitalised injury data and ARDD fatalities, 2021 (39,505 admitted; 1,130 road deaths).
The road toll is falling. The injury toll
The road toll is falling. The injury toll isn't.
Cycling injuries have more than doubled among
Cyclists aged 65 and over: the biggest rise of any group
I travel by: Pedal cyclist v
Older patients stay longer in hospital and are more likely to die
Pedestrians are 1 in 14 of the injured, but 1
in 4 of those who die in hospital
Pedestrians take up twice their share of hospital beds
Measure: 1 Admissions | 2 Bed days | 3 Deaths in hospital
For pedestrians over 75, one admission in 16 ends in death
open dot: all road users | dark dot + whisker: pedestrians
Apart from rare train collisions, a heavy vehicle or bus is the deadliest thing to be hit by
open: all road users | dark: pedestrians
In the month Australia locked down, crash
admissions fell by a third. Cyclist
April 2020: a third fewer crash admissions
Every road user went to hospital less in April 2020, except cyclists
Cyclist injuries were already rising. 2020 added to it.
Victoria had the largest rise in cyclist admissions in July-December 2020
hospitalised after road crashes at about the
same rate as everyone else. By 2021 the rate
First Nations hospitalisations nearly doubled; everyone else's rose 15%
Pedestrians are a bigger share of First Nations road-crash hospitalisations: 11% against 6%
In remote areas, First Nations people are 41% of those hospitalised after road crashes
The road toll isn't the whole story.
If you ride, you're part of a growing group.
If your parents walk, the danger isn't how often they're hit but
The roads are not equally safe for everyone, and counts alone hide
Team Shu · COS30045 Data Visualisation · Swinburne · 2026
